catalog_quote: Upper Faifi is a stress-to-weight language where the general rule is that the heaviest syllable in the word will be stressed (cf. A. H. Alfaifi 2022, discussed below). ... A short vowel is assigned one mora; a long vowel is assigned two morae. Furthermore, a coda will be assigned an extra mora. ... Syllables are classified by weight as light, heavy, and superheavy, with no more than one superheavy syllable occurring in each word. ... Stress is assigned to the heaviest syllable in the word. If a superheavy syllable appears in a word, it is stressed. ... Most importantly, word-final codas do not count for weight, and thus, a word-final syllable with a coda is not classified as heavy unless the nucleus is a long vowel. For instance, in a word like [ˈʔig.bil] ‘return’, the first syllable is stressed ... However, note that the word [ta.ˈfuːz] ‘win’ will stress the second syllable ... Additio…

new_statements.quote: Stress is assigned to the heaviest syllable in the word. If a superheavy syllable appears in a word, it is stressed. [...] Most importantly, word-final codas do not count for weight [...] Additionally, if there is more than one heavy syllable in the word, then stress is assigned to the leftmost heavy syllable, as in [ma.ˈfaː.tiː.ħin] 'keys'. If no heavy syllables appear in a word, then the penultimate syllable is stressed, as in [ka.ˈsa.fan] 'eclipsed'. A. H. Alfaifi (2022) reported different stress patterns regarding Central Faifi. In this variety, stress falls on the first syllable from the left edge of the word, irrespective of the weight of any other syllable after the initial one

new_statements.rule_in_words: Upper Faifi: quantity-sensitive. Stress the superheavy syllable (CVVC/CVCC) if present; otherwise the leftmost heavy syllable (CVV, or non-final CVC; word-final codas are weightless so final CVC is light but final CVV(C) is heavy); if the word has no heavy syllable, stress the penult. The same source reports, second-hand from A.H. Alfaifi's 2022 IU dissertation, that Central Faifi instead has fixed word-initial stress regardless of weight.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final coda consonants do not contribute weight (['ʔig.bil] initial stress vs [ta.'fuːz] final stress because of the long vowel); CVCC only word-finally with 1SG /-t/; at most one superheavy per word; authors flag that Central Faifi (A.H. Alfaifi 2022) has a different, initial-stress system and that 'the topic of stress across FA varieties needs further investigation'. Alfaifi & Davis 2022:101 had earlier declined to mark stress because 'the stress pattern of this dialect is in need of further study'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress; data are ~201 isolated citation-form words read three times by one 35-year-old male Upper Faifi speaker (linguist) recorded at U. Arizona; description is impressionistic/phonological (no acoustic stress measurements reported in 6.2).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted rule describes UPPER Faifi (higher-elevation villages of Jabal Fayfa; one speaker), following the Upper/Lower split of Alfaifi & Behnstedt 2010 and Alfaife 2018 (the latter describes Lower Faifi). A. H. Alfaifi 2022 (IU) describes CENTRAL Faifi and, per Alfaifi et al. 2025 and the dissertation abstract, finds fixed word-initial stress irrespective of weight, so the stress system differs by sub-dialect within glottocode faif1234 (Glottolog has no sub-dialect codes). A catalog entry should be tagged 'Upper Faifi' and note the conflicting Central Faifi report.

sources.note: Sec. 6.2 'Stress' (pp.195-196): Upper Faifi is 'stress-to-weight': stress the heaviest syllable; superheavy (CVVC, CVCC) always stressed; word-final codas are not moraic (['ʔig.bil] initial, [ta.'fuːz] final because of long V); if more than one heavy syllable, the LEFTMOST heavy is stressed ([ma.'faː.tiː.ħin]); if no heavy syllable, the penult ([ka.'sa.fan]). Then reports A. H. Alfaifi (2022) for Central Faifi: stress on the first syllable regardless of weight (['ja.guu.muun], ['śi.lii.hu]), 'highly unusual in Arabic'; 'the topic of stress across FA varieties needs further investigation'.
